world.title: Reimagining multilateralism for global sexual and reproductive rights - The BMJ
world.summary: Amid proposals to restructure the UN and merge UNFPA and UN Women, Clarisa Bencomo and colleagues argue that strong specialised multilateral institutions remain essential for advancing gender equality and sexual and reproductive health and rights For 80 years the United Nations (UN) system has been a venue for advancing the rights of women, girls, and, over time, LGBTQ+ individuals.12 Its support for laws, norms, policies, and programmes to improve gender equality and sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR, box 1) directly contributed to global decreases in maternal mortality (40%, 2000-23) and women’s and girls’ AIDS related mortality (58%, 2010-24), and halved the lifetime risk of maternal related death (2020-23).34 The features that helped the UN make progress on SRHR—specialised gender equality and SRHR agencies with complementary mandates; civil society contributions to knowledge production, norm setting, and accountability; and consensus based decision making—are being undermined and those gains reversed. Today’s the UN faces unprecedented crises. Member states owed a record $1.6bn in regular budget dues at the end of 2025, and by May 2026, the UN projected it would run out of money in August if member states didn’t pay up.5 Voluntary development funding is shrinking, and 2026 bilateral aid for health is projected to reach its lowest level in almost two decades, with reproductive and population health hardest hit.6 Anti-rights agendas are gaining ground.7891011 Imposed austerity measures, illicit financial flows, and an emerging debt crisis make women and girls in low and middle income countries especially vulnerable.12 The UN secretary general’s solution to this moment is UN80, a rushed package of restructuring and programmatic cuts.
